@graph.headline: Why Backtested Strategies Fail in Live Trading: The 5 Gaps Between the Lab and the Field

acceptedAnswer.text: Because the backtest was a laboratory and live trading is the field. The backtest filled orders at the signal price with costs roughly estimated, on clean historical data, in one past market regime, while following the rules perfectly. Live differs in five ways: the execution gap, the cost gap, the data gap, the regime gap, and the trader gap — you do not follow the rules like the backtest did.

mainEntity.name: Why did my backtest show great results but I am losing money live?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the tightness ratio: average win divided by per-trade friction. For a swing trader with wide targets, a fraction of a percent of slippage is noise; for a scalper, half a point of slippage per trade can be the entire edge — and frequency multiplies it. For Indian option buyers there is an extra layer: backtests built on mid-prices, but live you buy the ask and sell the bid, paying the full spread every round trip.

mainEntity.name: Does slippage really matter in backtesting?

acceptedAnswer.text: Entry slippage roughly balances out over many trades — you miss both ways. Stop-loss slippage is directional: gaps blow through stops in the losing direction, because the price motion that reaches a stop is by definition moving against you. A backtest assuming exact stop fills systematically understates the worst losses. The fix: add a stop-fill penalty in the backtest and reconcile your actual stop fills against it on every trade.

mainEntity.name: Why do my stops get filled worse than my entries?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with realistic practitioner estimates for your instrument, then run the double-cost stress test: re-run the backtest with every cost doubled — brokerage, charges, spread, slippage. If the strategy survives, it is robust to cost uncertainty; if it only works with perfect fills, it does not work.

mainEntity.name: How much slippage should I add to a backtest?

acceptedAnswer.text: In-sample, a strategy can memorize the sample's noise — patterns that existed by chance in that specific period. Out-of-sample is the first taste of data the strategy has never seen, and chance patterns do not repeat. Published research points the same way: in one academic study of 97 stock-return predictors, returns were about 26% lower out-of-sample (McLean and Pontiff, 2016).

mainEntity.name: Why do backtests work in-sample but fail out-of-sample?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some gap is normal: one practitioner's calibration framework reads live performance at 70–80% of the backtest as good, 50–70% as acceptable, below 50% as concerning, and a live strategy going negative when the backtest was positive as action required. If your gap is larger than the bands allow, work through the five gaps: execution, cost, data, regime, and the trader.

mainEntity.name: Why is there such a big gap between backtest and live performance?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The backtest never hesitated, never skipped a setup, never moved a stop, never revenge-traded. The moment you deviate from the plan, you are no longer trading the strategy the backtest validated. Forward-test at tiny size or on paper and measure your deviations from the plan before you size up.

mainEntity.name: Does a backtest account for emotions?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A backtest replays history — fast, but it carries all four structural gaps (execution, cost, data, regime). Paper trading runs forward, live, without capital — slow, but it removes look-ahead risk by construction and gives you real-time fills and real data messiness. The honest funnel uses both: backtest, stress test, out-of-sample, paper, then live small.
